cases.title: A trusted handoff queue
cases.request: Create a substantive PRD from this product discussion. Make it useful to a planning agent, preserving unresolved decisions.
cases.metadata: P1; 2026-09-07 09:00 Asia/Singapore; product brainstorm; Maya product, Leo engineering, Sam customer success; calendar also lists Noor but no speech or attendance evidence for Noor.
cases.transcript:
[00:12] Maya: Our hypothesis is that customer handoffs fail because nobody knows who owns the next step. I want a PRD today, not a commitment to build everything.
[01:04] Sam: Three account managers told me they lose thirty minutes finding the latest promise. That is anecdotal; I have not measured it.
[02:19] Leo: The spreadsheet export actually includes an owner column. It is often blank. This might be a workflow problem rather than a missing field.
[03:10] Maya: So our first version is a queue of outstanding commitments with an owner and a source passage. We should let someone mark an item disputed.
[04:02] Sam: Please do not automatically email customers. A tentative idea in a call can look like a promise out of context.
[05:40] Leo: Syncing ownership back to CRM would take a separate integration. We can link to the record first.
[06:11] Maya: Agreed. Read-only CRM links for the pilot, no automatic email. The interface should show proposed versus confirmed commitments.
[07:24] Sam: Can we promise fifty percent less handoff time?
[07:38] Maya: Not yet. Measure the baseline. A two-week pilot is a suggestion, not a launch date.
[08:22] Leo: Customer workspace permissions must follow the source. A manager should not discover another account through search.
[09:35] Maya: Write the draft, show alternatives and what we still need to validate. Let us decide pilot accounts next week.
cases.companyContext: Synthetic record D1: product analytics dashboard, 2026-09-06: 18 weekly active account managers; handoff duration is not instrumented. Synthetic D2: access policy: source-workspace membership required for every retrieved commitment. No further documents available.
must: No invented fifty-percent target or committed pilot date
Separate missing ownership behavior from missing-field hypothesis
Include measurable acceptance examples and permission boundaries
Noor not asserted to have attended

cases.title: Reliable commitment events
cases.request: Create an engineering RFC from this discussion and research the contested reliability claim.
cases.metadata: E1; 2026-09-07 10:30 Asia/Singapore; architecture review; Leo engineer, Priya platform, Maya product.
cases.transcript:
[00:20] Leo: We commit a new commitment to Postgres and then publish its event. Last Thursday the process died between those two operations.
[01:06] Priya: The retry produced the opposite problem later: two notifications. I think an outbox gives exactly-once delivery.
[02:10] Leo: I think it gives us a durable intent to publish, but consumers still need deduplication. Please check the claim.
[03:30] Maya: For the pilot, no customer emails. Losing an internal queue update is worse than a minute of delay.
[04:28] Priya: We could poll an outbox table or use CDC. We already operate Postgres, but not a CDC pipeline.
[05:17] Leo: Let us propose polling first. Record and outbox insert in one database transaction; worker retries publication. We have not agreed to a broker yet.
[06:50] Priya: If the worker crashes after publish but before marking sent, there is a duplicate. The event needs an identifier that survives retries.
[07:45] Maya: Is under sixty seconds reasonable?
[07:52] Leo: A candidate target, yes. We have not measured peak throughput.
[08:30] Priya: We must not change committed event payloads on retries. Also how long do we retain failed entries? Open question.
[09:08] Leo: Please draft an RFC with failure modes, tests, migration and a rollback plan. Mark the unresolved decisions so a coding agent does not invent them.
cases.companyContext: Synthetic A1 architecture note dated 2026-09-05: Postgres 17, workers can run scheduled jobs, no existing CDC infrastructure. Synthetic I1 incident note: one missing event and two duplicate internal notifications observed; no measured loss rate or peak volume.
must: Outbox does not promise exactly-once end-to-end delivery
Broker and retention remain open
Crash-after-publish test and idempotency included
60-second target labeled proposed

cases.title: Finding the promise, not another dashboard
cases.request: Analyze these customer interview notes for product discovery. Recommend a useful next experiment.
cases.metadata: C1; 2026-09-07 13:00 Asia/Singapore; one interview, one participant Elena operations lead; interviewer Sam; recording consent confirmed in fixture.
cases.transcript:
[00:10] Sam: How do you prepare for a customer handoff today?
[00:42] Elena: I search Slack, open the call notes, then ask the rep. The notes say next steps but rarely explain whether the customer actually agreed.
[02:01] Sam: Would an AI dashboard solve that?
[02:15] Elena: Maybe. Honestly I do not want another dashboard. I want the exact sentence where someone promised something.
[03:27] Sam: How often is this happening?
[03:46] Elena: It felt daily last month during renewals. I have not counted. This week was quiet.
[04:10] Sam: Can you show me the last time?
[04:33] Elena: Yesterday I spent about twenty minutes finding a pricing exception. In the end it was a suggestion, not approved pricing.
[05:52] Sam: Would you pay fifty dollars a seat for a queue?
[06:04] Elena: I am not the buyer. I could try it with two people, but security would need to approve the transcript access.
[07:16] Sam: What do you already use?
[07:30] Elena: A pinned Slack thread. It works for small accounts. It falls apart when six teams get involved.
[08:20] Sam: Anything that would make a new system worse?
[08:37] Elena: If it turns a maybe into a commitment. Or shares a sensitive account with the wrong team.
[09:15] Sam: We can test a source-linked queue in a prototype.
[09:27] Elena: Yes, if I can still use Slack. Do not call that a purchase promise.
cases.companyContext: Synthetic interview tracker C-17 confirms a single participant. No other interviews, purchase authority, measured frequency or competitor evaluation is supplied.
must: Single participant and leading questions acknowledged
Interest not willingness to pay
Preserve contradiction of daily feeling versus quiet week
Experiment tests source evidence and existing Slack workflow

cases.title: A pilot opportunity, not a committed deal
cases.request: Analyze this discovery call and draft a useful follow-up. Use the CRM fixture to check the deal claims.
cases.metadata: S1; 2026-09-07 15:00 Asia/Singapore; seller Aiden, buyer operations Jo; CFO invited but absent according to Jo.
cases.transcript:
[00:18] Jo: Our CFO could not join. I can sponsor a pilot, but I cannot sign the annual contract.
[01:21] Aiden: Your team loses five hours a week preparing handoffs, right?
[01:42] Jo: That was one bad week. Usually it is closer to two, and I am estimating.
[02:50] Jo: Source links matter more than the prose. My team needs to check what the client actually said.
[03:28] Aiden: We are fully certified and can put you live next month.
[03:59] Jo: Please send the security evidence. We will not upload customer transcripts until security signs off.
[05:02] Aiden: Could we say thirty seats at twelve thousand a year?
[05:22] Jo: That is within the range I might propose, not an approved budget. Start with five pilot users.
[06:41] Jo: Procurement meets late in October, but the date is not confirmed.
[07:14] Aiden: I will send a draft pilot plan and security pack on Thursday.
[07:58] Jo: Yes. Include what gets stored and what gets deleted. We are also considering keeping our current manual process.
[08:43] Aiden: Can I put you down as committed?
[08:52] Jo: No. Let us verify the security requirements and decide the pilot first.
